Council of Chalcedon
kal-SEE-don
proper noun (church history / Christology)
Named after Chalcedon, a city in Bithynia on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus opposite Constantinople (modern Kadıköy, Turkey); from Greek Chalkedōn (Χαλκηδών); the Fourth Ecumenical Council convened there in October 451 AD under Emperor Marcian, attended by approximately 520–630 bishops; it produced the Chalcedonian Definition (“the Tome of Leo” was the Western contribution), which became the permanent Christological standard of orthodox Christianity

See also: Council of Chalcedon

Biblical Definition

The Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) settled the question that had convulsed the church for a century: how are the two natures of Christ — divine and human — related in the one person of the Son? The council's Definition answered in four negative adverbs that have governed orthodox Christology ever since: the two natures are united “without confusion, without change, without division, without separation” (asynchytōs, atreoptōs, adiairetōs, achōristōs). The first two guard against Eutychianism, which collapsed the natures into a blended third nature; the last two guard against Nestorianism, which divided the natures so thoroughly that the person threatened to become two. Against both errors, Chalcedon held that the eternal Son assumed a fully human nature — body and rational soul — into union with His divine nature, the two natures remaining distinct and complete but united in the one person. The scriptural roots are clear: John 1:14 (“the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”) establishes the genuine humanity; Philippians 2:6–7 shows the Son existing in divine form and taking human form; Hebrews 2:14 grounds the atonement in His sharing our flesh and blood. Every subsequent Christological debate in the church — from Monophysitism through Monothelitism through modern Kenotic theories — is evaluated against the Chalcedonian standard. The 1689 LBCF 8.2 affirms the Chalcedonian pattern without citation: “two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, the Godhead and the manhood, were inseparably joined together in one person.”

Webster 1828 Definition

COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON: the Fourth Ecumenical Council (451 AD) convened at Chalcedon in Bithynia; produced the Chalcedonian Definition affirming Christ's two natures — divine and human — united in one person without confusion, change, division, or separation; the permanent Christological standard of orthodox Christianity.

COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON. n. The Fourth Ecumenical Council of the Christian Church, assembled at Chalcedon (Bithynia) in October 451 AD under the presidency of Emperor Marcian; attended by approximately 520–630 bishops primarily from the Eastern church, with Western representation through papal legates carrying Pope Leo I's Tome.

The council responded to two Christological errors: Eutychianism, which taught that the human nature was absorbed into the divine after the Incarnation, producing a single blended nature; and Nestorianism (condemned at Ephesus 431), which so distinguished the natures as to threaten the unity of the person. The Chalcedonian Definition navigated between them with the four negative adverbs: asynchytōs (without confusion), atreoptōs (without change), adiairetōs (without division), achōristōs (without separation).

Leo's Tome (Letter 28, 449 AD) provided the Christological framework: each nature retains its own properties while acting in communion with the other through the communicatio idiomatum (communication of attributes). What belongs to the divine nature and what belongs to the human nature may be predicated of the one person.

The council's rejection of the title Theotokos (God-bearer) applied to Mary was NOT among its decisions; it had been affirmed at Ephesus 431 and Chalcedon upheld it. Chalcedon's ecumenical authority is recognized by Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and all Reformation confessional churches. The non-Chalcedonian Oriental churches (Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian, Syriac Orthodox) accept Cyril's one-nature language but the modern assessment is that the differences are partly terminological.

The 1689 LBCF 8.2 is a Chalcedonian confession: “The Son of God, the second person in the Trinity, being very and eternal God, of one substance, and equal with the Father, did when the fullness of time was come, take upon Him man's nature, with all the essential properties and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin.”

Key Scripture

John 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."

Phil 2:6 — "Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:"

Phil 2:7 — "But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:"

Heb 2:14 — "Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;"

Modern Corruption

Modern Kenotic Christology softens the Chalcedonian Definition by having the Son surrender divine attributes at the Incarnation; liberal theology treats Chalcedon as a Greek philosophical imposition on simple Jewish Christianity; both empty the Definition of its content and compromise the atonement.

expand to see more

Kenotic Christology (from the nineteenth century, popularized by Göttingen theologians) proposed that the Son emptied Himself of His divine attributes (omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence) at the Incarnation in order to become genuinely human — appealing to the ekenosen of Philippians 2:7. The Chalcedonian answer is that the emptying is of glory and the exercise of divine prerogatives, not of the divine nature itself: the Son took a human nature, not a reduced divine nature. A Christ who lacked omniscience would be incapable of knowing the Father perfectly, of securing a covenant-keeping relationship with God on behalf of sinners, or of making the infinite satisfaction that an infinite God requires. The Chalcedonian two-nature framework preserves both the genuine humanity (He grew in wisdom, Luke 2:52 — per His human nature) and the undiminished divinity (He knew what was in man, John 2:25 — per His divine nature) without contradiction.

Liberal Protestantism from Harnack onward treated the Chalcedonian Definition as a corruption of the “simple Gospel” by Greek metaphysics — the church had replaced the prophetic Galilean teacher with a Greek philosophical abstraction. The corrective is historical rather than merely theological: Chalcedon did not impose Greek philosophy on biblical data; it used available Greek philosophical vocabulary to preserve biblical data against heresy. The alternative to Chalcedonian precision was not a simpler Jesus but one of the Christological errors the Definition excluded. A Christ who is not fully divine cannot save; a Christ who is not fully human cannot substitute. Chalcedon is the minimum grammar necessary to say what the New Testament says about Jesus.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Chalkedōn (city in Bithynia); the four negative adverbs asynchytōs, atreoptōs, adiairetōs, achōristōs (without confusion, change, division, separation); the terminological outcome of a century of Christological controversy from Arius (325) through Apollinarius, Nestorius, and Eutyches to the Definition of 451.

expand to see more

Chalcedon (451) as the fourth ecumenical council — preceded by Nicaea (325, Arianism condemned), Constantinople I (381, Pneumatomachi/Macedonians condemned), and Ephesus (431, Nestorianism condemned); each council addressed a specific heretical distortion of the biblical Christ and produced a permanent doctrinal standard

Asynchytōs (without confusion/mixture) — the first negative adverb, aimed at Eutychianism; the two natures do not blend into a third thing; the divine remains fully divine and the human remains fully human even in the union; the Incarnation does not produce a demigod

Atreoptōs (without change) — the second adverb; neither nature undergoes alteration by the union; the divine nature does not become a lesser thing, and the human nature is not elevated to divinity; the union is personal, not essential

Adiairetōs (without division) and achōristōs (without separation) — the third and fourth adverbs, aimed at Nestorian tendencies; though the natures remain distinct, there is no division into two persons or separation of the natures in operation; the one person acts through both natures in every act

Leo's Tome (449 AD) — Pope Leo I's letter to Flavian of Constantinople, which provided the Western Christological framework later incorporated into the Definition; Leo's formula “each form does the acts which belong to it, in communion with the other” is the clearest statement of communicatio idiomatum in the patristic period

Usage

"The Chalcedonian Definition is the ecumenical consensus that unites Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and all confessional Protestant churches — which is extraordinary given the depth of disagreements on other matters. Reformed preaching and catechesis should root Christological teaching in this Definition not as an appeal to tradition over Scripture but as the church's summary of what the New Testament actually teaches. When the Definition is taught, congregations have the grammar to resist modern Kenotic compromises and popular portrayals of Jesus that flatten Him into either pure God or mere man."

"The pastoral importance of Chalcedon is most evident in soteriology: the atonement requires both natures. A merely human Christ could not make infinite satisfaction for sin (the infinite honor of God requires an infinite person); a merely divine Christ could not die (divinity is impassible and immortal). Only the person who is both — the God-man of Chalcedon — can do what the cross required: die as man, with infinite value as God. Strip either nature and the Gospel unravels. This is why every generation of pastoral ministry must be Chalcedonian."

"In culture, Chalcedonian Christology is the answer to the two perennial popular distortions of Jesus: the “inspirational human teacher” of progressive Christianity (who cannot be the Son of God and cannot save) and the “divine figure who only seemed human” of early Docetism (who cannot die and cannot sympathize). The Definition holds the tension not as a philosophical puzzle but as the grammar of the Gospel: He was born of a woman (Gal 4:4), and He is God blessed forever (Rom 9:5)."
